'''''Lolium rigidum''''' is a [[species]] of  annual [[grass]]. Common names by which it is known include '''annual ryegrass''', a name also given to [[Lolium multiflorum|Italian ryegrass]] (''Lolium multiflorum''), '''rigid ryegrass''', '''stiff darnel''', '''Swiss ryegrass''' and '''Wimmera ryegrass'''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/03030800-0b07-490a-8d04-0605030c0f01/media/Html/Lolium_rigidum.htm |title=Annual ryegrass: ''Lolium rigidum'' |work=Weeds of Australia |publisher=Biosecurity Queensland |accessdate=6 December 2015}}</ref> It is a native of southern Europe, northern Africa, the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent and is grown as a forage crop, particularly in Australia, where it is also a serious and economically damaging crop weed.

==Description==
''Lolium rigidum'' is an annual grass that grows in open tussocks. It has fibrous roots and can grow up to a metre tall. The plant form is usually erect but may be prostrate. The stems are often geniculate (with a knee-like bend) and are purplish at the base. The leaves are {{convert|5|to|25|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long, and {{convert|3|to|5|mm|in|2|abbr=on}} wide; the upper surface is glossy dark green, flat and hairless with longitudinal veins, and the underside is shiny and smooth.
[[File:Lolium rigidum spikelets5 annotated (7370409964).jpg|thumb|left|165px|Annotated spikelet]]
The young leaves are rolled when in bud, the auricles are small and the ligule is white and translucent, wider than it is long. The unbranched flower spike is up to {{convert|30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long, with the [[Poaceae#Description|spikelets]] on alternating sides and edgeways-on to the [[rachis]] (stem), pressed into recesses in the stem.

The spikelets bear up to twelve florets, mostly with a single [[glume]], with only the terminal floret having two. The glumes are up to three-quarters the length of the spikelet; their outer surface is finely ribbed with longitudinal veins. There is no [[Awn (botany)|awn]], the [[Lemma (botany)|lemma]] is oblong and has five nerves and the [[Palea (botany)|palea]] is a similar shape with two nerve and a few fine hairs. The three anthers are yellow.<ref name=CABI>{{cite journal |url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/31167 |title=''Lolium rigidum'' (rigid ryegrass) |journal=Invasive Species Compendium |date=2021 |publisher=CABI |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.31167 |accessdate=6 December 2015|url-access=subscription |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Lolium rigidum'' is a native of the Mediterranean area. Its natural range includes Western, Southern and Central Europe, northern Africa, the Near East, western Asia and the Indian sub-continent. It has spread to many other parts of the world and is considered invasive in some regions. It is planted in Australia as a forage crop but not usually in Europe.<ref name=Boller>{{cite book|author1=Boller, Beat |author2=Posselt, Ulrich K. |author3=Veronesi, Fabio |title=Fodder Crops and Amenity Grasses |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lMVfkHFjkZUC&pg=PA213 |year=2010 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4419-0760-8 |pages=213–216}}</ref> It was introduced as a forage crop in Australia around 1880, but has since proven to be an economically damaging weed that infests other more important crops, such as [[canola]] and [[wheat]].<ref name= Murrumbidgee>{{cite report| url=http://archive.lls.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0008/495332/archive-annual-ryegrass.pdf| title=Annual ryegrass (Lolium rigidum)| series= Best Management Practices for Dryland Cropping Systems| author= Murrumbidgee Catchment Management Authority| date=2008 | access-date=31 July 2021}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Lolium rigidum'' is a diploid grass with a chromosome number of n=7 (2n=14). It exhibits much genetic variability and grows readily in a variety of situations and habitats. It can hybridise with both [[Lolium perenne|perennial]] (''L. perenne'') and [[Lolium multiflorum|Italian ryegrass]] (''L. multiflorum''), as well as some species of ''[[Festuca]]''. It propagates solely by seed; freshly shed seed displays [[dormancy]].<ref name=CABI/> It is sometimes infected by a rust fungus which has an inhibitory effect on the growth of clovers.<ref name=HerbiGuide>{{cite web |url=http://www.herbiguide.com.au/Descriptions/hg_Annual_Ryegrass.htm |title=Annual ryegrass |publisher=HerbiGuide |accessdate=6 December 2015}}</ref>

The flower spike of ''L. rigidum'' may become infected by a certain species of bacteria, which results in the production of [[corynetoxin]]s which are toxic to livestock; ingestion of infected material causes a disease, known as [[annual ryegrass toxicity]] or annual ryegrass staggers, which is known to occur in the west and south of Australia and in South Africa.<ref name=Merck/> The infection is caused by the bacterium ''[[Rathayibacter toxicus]]'', which is introduced into the grass by the [[nematode]] ''[[Anguina funesta]]''. This nematode causes galls on the grass flower spikes and it is in these that the bacteria multiply. Infected galls are present in the winter, but become more toxic as the inflorescence dies in spring. The disease occurs when the pasture is grazed at this toxic stage. Topping the pasture before grazing may prevent the condition, but the seed heads are still toxic when preserved as hay.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.sheepconnectsa.com.au/technical-information/monitor-stock-for-annual-ryegrass-toxicity |title=Annual ryegrass toxicity |publisher=SheepConnect |accessdate=11 December 2015}}</ref> The symptoms of poisoning are neurological, often causing a mortality rate of forty to fifty percent in infected animals.<ref name=Merck>{{cite web |url=http://www.merckvetmanual.com/mvm/toxicology/ryegrass_toxicity/annual_ryegrass_staggers.html |title=Annual ryegrass staggers |author=Simpson, Wayne |date=1 August 2013 |publisher=Merck |accessdate=9 December 2015 |archive-date=11 December 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151211045645/http://www.merckvetmanual.com/mvm/toxicology/ryegrass_toxicity/annual_ryegrass_staggers.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

''L. rigidum'' is susceptible to infection by [[ergot]] (''Claviceps purpurea''), and also by [[take-all]] fungus (''Gaeumannomyces graminis'') which can cause serious losses in cereal crops.<ref name=CABI/>

==Uses==
''Lolium rigidum'' is grown as a forage crop in suitable areas. About 80% of the seed germinates in the autumn, soon after the first significant rains, and about 5% may remain dormant for twelve months. The plant has vigorous growth, and flowering is initiated when the day length is at least eight hours. This means that the crop has a relatively uniform flowering period in late winter/early spring.<ref name=HerbiGuide/>

==Damaging effects==
Because ''L. rigidum'' has been grown as a forage crop in southern Australia since the nineteenth century and seeds readily, it grows ubiquitously in the region with large, genetically diverse populations. Now that arable crops are increasingly being grown, it has become an important weed of these crops.<ref name=pia/> The main reason for its success in competing with crops is its ability to produce prolific numbers of seeds per plant – up to 45,000 seeds per {{cvt|1|m2}} – and also its ability to compete with crops at a very early stage of their life cycle.<ref name=wa/>

In addition, it serves as a host for species of the bacteria [[Rathayibacter toxicus]] (formerly [[Clavibacter]]), which cause [[annual ryegrass toxicity]] (ARGT), and can be infected by the poisonous [[ergot fungus]],<ref name=wa>{{cite web | title=Annual ryegrass | website=Agriculture and Food|publisher= Western Australia. [[Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (Western Australia)|Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development]] | date=7 December 2020 | url=https://www.agric.wa.gov.au/grains-research-development/annual-ryegrass | access-date=31 July 2021}}</ref> which causes [[ergotism]] in humans and other mammals.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ianrpubs.unl.edu/live/ec1880/build/ec1880.pdf|title=Ergot of Small Grain Cereals and Grasses and Its Health Effects on Humans and Livestock |last1=Wegulo |first1=Stephen N |last2=Carlson |first2=Michael P.  |date=2011 |website=University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension}}</ref>

Attempts to control it with [[herbicide]] have met with an unexpectedly high level of [[herbicide resistance]]. Over 90% of plants in some populations are tolerant to some of the widely used herbicides. Instead of wiping out the ''L. rigidum'', the herbicides have resulted in the selection of resistant genotypes.<ref name=pia>{{cite web |url= http://plantsinaction.science.uq.edu.au/edition1/?q=content/20-1-1-lolium-rigidum-australia-very-resistance-prone-weed |title=''Lolium rigidum'' in Australia: a very resistance prone weed! |work=Plants in Action |accessdate=8 December 2015}}</ref><ref name=wa/> Glyphosate resistance was first discovered in populations of rigid ryegrass in Australia in 1996. Since then, glyphosate resistance has been detected in additional populations of rigid ryegrass and Italian ryegrass in several other countries.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Preston |first1=Christopher |year=1996 |title=Multiple resistance to dissimilar herbicide chemistries in a biotype of Lolium rigidum due to enhanced activity of several herbicide degrading enzymes |journal=Pesticide Biochemistry and Physiology |volume=54 |issue=2 |pages=123-124 |doi=10.1006/pest.1996.0016 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0048357596900164|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Powles |first1=Stephen |year=1998 |title=Evolved resistance to glyphosate in rigid ryegrass (Lolium rigidum) in Australia  |journal=Weed Science |volume=46 |issue=5 |pages=604-607 |doi=10.1017/S0043174500091165 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4045968|author-link=Stephen Powles}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Preston |first1=Christopher |year=2009 |title=A Decade of Glyphosate-Resistant Lolium around the World: Mechanisms, Genes, Fitness, and Agronomic Management |journal=Weed Science |volume=57 |issue=4 |pages=123-124 |doi=10.1614/WS-08-181.1 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40586851}}</ref> Possible [[bioherbicide]]s are being explored, including ''[[Pyrenophora seminiperda]]'', a fungus.<ref name= Murrumbidgee/> 


''L. rigidum'' has become one of the most serious and economically damaging weeds in southern Australia. A 2021 study listed annual ryegrass as fourth on the list of [[invasive species]] which cost Australian farmers the most over a 60-year period, at over a billion Australian dollars.<ref>{{cite web | last=Khan | first=Jo | title=Invasive species have cost Australia $390 billion in the past 60 years, study shows | website=ABC News| publisher= [[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]] | date=31 July 2021 | url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/science/2021-07-30/invasive-species-cost-billions-australia/100333710 | access-date=30 July 2021}}</ref>
